blocks.text: **Adrenal insufficiency** is failure of the adrenal cortex to secrete enough **cortisol and/or aldosterone**. It is potentially fatal and its presentation is notoriously variable, so think of it in anyone with **unexplained fatigue, hyponatraemia or hypotension**.

blocks.title: Levels at which the axis can fail
rows: Pituitary tumour, surgery, radiotherapy, Sheehan’s syndrome

blocks.text: **Addison’s disease** = **primary** adrenocortical failure, with destruction of the whole cortex and a **raised ACTH**. It is rare (incidence about **3–4 per million per year**) with a **marked female preponderance**. Either glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid deficiency may appear first, but eventually **both** classes of corticosteroid fail.
Steroids are essential for life: untreated Addison’s disease is life threatening, and replacement is **lifelong**.

“Adrenal insufficiency” is not the same as “Addison’s disease”. The **commonest form overall is secondary** (ACTH deficiency), usually from inappropriate withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids or a pituitary tumour. Addison’s disease and congenital adrenal hyperplasia are **rare** causes. Davidson groups steroid-withdrawal suppression under secondary (low ACTH) failure; Zero to Finals labels it tertiary.

The adrenal cortex works as **two functional units**. The **zona glomerulosa** makes **aldosterone** under the **renin–angiotensin system** (angiotensin II is the main stimulus). The **zonae fasciculata and reticularis** make **cortisol and adrenal androgens** under **ACTH**, as part of the HPA axis: hypothalamic CRH drives pituitary ACTH, which drives cortisol, and cortisol feeds back negatively on both.
Destruction must be extensive: around **90% of adrenal tissue** has to be lost (e.g. by metastases) before insufficiency appears.

blocks.title: What each hormone deficit explains
rows: Peaks on waking, surges with stress or illness; gluconeogenic; limits inflammation
Malaise, weight loss, **hypoglycaemia**, **dilutional** hyponatraemia; poor tolerance of stress, so illness can tip into crisis
Renal mineralocorticoid receptor: retains Na, excretes K and H+
Main androgen source in adult women
Less body hair and reduced libido, especially in women
Loss of cortisol negative feedback; ACTH and other POMC-derived peptides carry MSH-like sequences

blocks.text: **Pigmentation and hyperkalaemia both point to the adrenal (primary) level**: pigmentation needs high ACTH, and hyperkalaemia needs aldosterone loss, neither of which occurs when the problem is lack of ACTH.
Hyponatraemia does **not** tell you about mineralocorticoid status: it occurs with cortisol lack (dilutional) as well as aldosterone lack (depletional).

blocks.title: Causes of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease)
items: **Autoimmune adrenalitis**: sporadic or part of a polyglandular syndrome; **> 90% of UK cases**; autoantibodies target **21-hydroxylase**
**Infection**: **tuberculosis** (rising where HIV is common), **HIV/AIDS**, fungi (histoplasmosis), CMV
**Malignant infiltration**: metastatic carcinoma (lung, breast, stomach, colon); lymphoma (rare)
**Haemorrhage/infarction**: **Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome** (adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal sepsis), adrenal vein thrombosis
**Deposition**: amyloidosis, haemochromatosis, sarcoidosis
**Surgery**: bilateral adrenalectomy

**Blocked steroid synthesis**: congenital adrenal hyperplasia; drugs such as **metyrapone, ketoconazole and etomidate** (etomidate even after one dose); rifampicin and anticonvulsants are also implicated

blocks.title: Causes of secondary/tertiary insufficiency (low ACTH)
items: **Withdrawal of long-term suppressive glucocorticoids**: the commonest cause of adrenal insufficiency overall
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease: tumour, pituitary surgery, radiotherapy, infection, infarction
**Sheehan’s syndrome**: pituitary necrosis after massive postpartum haemorrhage

blocks.title: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes
rows: Autosomal dominant; HLA-DR3 and CTLA-4 associations
Addison’s, **hypoparathyroidism**, **chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis**, nail dystrophy, dental enamel hypoplasia
Addison’s with hypothyroidism or Graves’, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, coeliac disease

blocks.text: In **children**, the commonest cause of primary adrenal insufficiency is **congenital adrenal hyperplasia**. In a patient with Addison’s plus **degenerative neurological symptoms**, exclude **adrenoleukodystrophy**.

“Most common cause” depends on the question. **Overall**: steroid withdrawal (secondary). **Addison’s in the UK/industrialised world**: autoimmune. **Addison’s worldwide**: tuberculosis (Step-Up). Kumar adds that TB is a growing cause where HIV is common.

Steroid suppression threshold: Davidson says withdrawal crisis is likely after **> 3 weeks** of oral/systemic steroid, **repeated courses within a year**, or **> 7.5 mg prednisolone/day**. Pocket Medicine warns suppression may follow **≤ 2 weeks**; inhaled and topical steroids can also suppress the axis. Learn Davidson’s criteria.

blocks.note: Look at: CT showing **bilateral adrenal calcification**, a pointer to tuberculous Addison’s disease.

blocks.text: The chronic presentation is **insidious and non-specific**: lethargy, depression, anorexia and **weight loss**, which is a uniform feature of primary disease. Patients are often mislabelled as having chronic fatigue syndrome or depression. **Postural hypotension** from salt and water loss is an early sign.

blocks.title: Features grouped by mechanism
rows: Anorexia with weight loss; tiredness and weakness; vomiting; altered bowel habit (either direction); low BP on standing or frank shock; hypoglycaemia, dilutional hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia; psychiatric features (depression, confusion, psychosis); amenorrhoea
Hypotension, shock, depletional hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, salt craving
Pigmentation of sun-exposed areas, pressure areas (elbows, knees), palmar creases, knuckles, mucous membranes, conjunctivae and recent scars
Reduced body hair and libido, especially in women

blocks.title: How often features occur
items: Weakness/fatigue ~95%; hyponatraemia ~75%; weight loss ~70%; nausea and vomiting ~50% each
Dull slate-grey/brown **pigmentation**: the predominant sign in **> 90%** (Kumar)
**Postural systolic hypotension** in **80–90%**, even when supine BP is normal
**Vitiligo** in **10–20%** of autoimmune Addison’s disease

blocks.title: Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis
items: **Circulatory shock** with severe hypotension; may be the **first presentation**
**Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia**, sometimes **hypoglycaemia** and hypercalcaemia
Vomiting, diarrhoea, muscle cramps, **abdominal pain that can mimic an acute abdomen**, unexplained fever, reduced consciousness
Precipitants: intercurrent illness, infection, trauma, surgery, or **abrupt stopping of long-term steroids**

blocks.text: In **older people** adrenal insufficiency is often insidious, presenting as tiredness, drowsiness, delirium, falls, immobility and orthostatic hypotension.
Secondary insufficiency mimics Addison’s disease but has **no pigmentation**, **preserved mineralocorticoid function**, and often **other pituitary hormone deficiencies**.

blocks.note: Look at: symptoms and signs of Addison’s disease: weight loss, pigmented new scars, palmar creases and buccal mucosa, postural hypotension, vitiligo, loss of body hair.
Look at: photo of **skin-crease pigmentation** from high ACTH in Addison’s disease, beside **vitiligo** of organ-specific autoimmune disease.

blocks.text: In suspected **adrenal crisis, never delay treatment for results**. Store a random blood sample for cortisol (and ACTH if possible), then give hydrocortisone. Do a 30-minute Synacthen test first only if the patient’s condition allows it without harmful delay. In a **chronic** presentation, investigate **before** treating.

blocks.title: Step 1: is cortisol secretion inadequate?
items: **Random cortisol** is usually low but can sit in the reference range yet be inappropriately low for a sick patient. Only a value **> 500 nmol/L (> 18 μg/dL)** effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency
Pocket Medicine: early-morning cortisol **< 3 μg/dL** is virtually diagnostic
**Short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test**: **250 μg ACTH1–24 IM**, any time of day; cortisol at **0 and 30 min**, plus ACTH at 0 min (on ice) if Addison’s is being considered
Normal = cortisol **> 500 nmol/L at baseline or at 30 min**; the **increment is not a criterion**

blocks.title: Step 2: primary or secondary?
items: **Plasma ACTH**: **high** in Addison’s disease (K&C Essentials: > 80 ng/L at 0900 with low or low-normal cortisol); **low** in ACTH deficiency
**Supine plasma renin and aldosterone**: mineralocorticoid deficiency shows **high renin** with **low or low-normal aldosterone**
Electrolytes cannot assess mineralocorticoid status reliably; hyperkalaemia is common but not universal

blocks.title: Step 3: what is the cause?
items: **Adrenal autoantibodies** (adrenal cortex, 21-hydroxylase): positive in most autoimmune cases (about 80–90%)
Antibody-negative: **CT/MRI of the adrenals**. Autoimmune glands are small and non-calcified; metastases, haemorrhage, infection or deposition enlarge them
**Tuberculosis** causes **adrenal calcification** on plain X-ray, ultrasound or CT
**HIV test** if risk factors are present
In autoimmune disease, **screen** for thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and type 1 diabetes
Secondary disease: pituitary work-up including **MRI**

blocks.title: Supportive routine results
items: **Hyponatraemia** (may be the only clue), **hyperkalaemia**, **raised urea**
Hypoglycaemia; hypercalcaemia occasionally
Eosinophilia, lymphocytosis, ± neutropenia; anaemia may appear after rehydration

blocks.alt: Algorithm: if shocked, store blood and give IV hydrocortisone and saline. If stable, short Synacthen test: cortisol over 500 nmol/L excludes; otherwise high ACTH means primary, low ACTH means secondary.

blocks.text: Limits of the Synacthen test: it fails in **both primary and chronic secondary** disease, so it does not tell you the level (measure ACTH). It relies on adrenal atrophy, so it can be **normal in acute ACTH deficiency** (e.g. pituitary apoplexy). All glucocorticoids, including creams, inhalers and drops, affect the result.

Synacthen cut-offs differ between books. **Davidson**: normal if cortisol > 500 nmol/L at baseline or 30 min, and the rise is not a criterion. K&C Essentials: basal > 170 **and** 30-min > 600 nmol/L. Zero to Finals uses “failure to double”. Use Davidson’s rule in exams.

The **long Synacthen test** (prolonged ACTH infusion) used to separate primary from secondary failure, because atrophic adrenals eventually respond. It is now largely obsolete because ACTH can be measured directly.

blocks.note: Look at: short ACTH stimulation curves. A normal subject’s cortisol rises into the reference range, while the Addison’s patient’s response is **decreased (blunted)**.

blocks.title: Adrenal crisis (Davidson Box 18.44)
rows: **IV 0.9% saline** to normalise BP and pulse (K&C Essentials: 1 L over 30–60 min, then 2–4 L over 12–24 h)
**IV hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg stat**, then **100 mg four times daily** for 12–24 h; then 50–100 mg IM four times daily until oral therapy is reliable
Raise Na by **no more than 10 mmol/L per day** (risk of pontine demyelination)
**Fludrocortisone not needed acutely**: high-dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid action. Kumar: start it before discharge
Look for a precipitant such as infection; consider adrenal or pituitary pathology

blocks.title: Long-term replacement (Davidson doses)
rows: **15–20 mg/day** in divided doses, e.g. 10 mg on waking + 5 mg at ~15:00
Clinically: weight gain suggests over-replacement; persistent lethargy or pigmentation suggests under-dosing or poor absorption. Serum cortisol is not usually helpful
**0.05–0.15 mg/day**; virtually all primary cases; **not needed in secondary**
BP, electrolytes, plasma renin. Kumar: no postural fall > 10 mmHg systolic after 2 min standing, renin suppressed towards high-normal
50 mg/day in some women with low libido/fatigue
Weak evidence; may cause acne or hirsutism

blocks.title: Sick-day rules and safety (Davidson Box 18.40)
items: **Febrile illness**: **double** the hydrocortisone dose
**Minor surgery**: hydrocortisone 100 mg IM with the premedication
**Major surgery**: 100 mg four times daily for 24 h, then 50 mg IM four times daily until tablets can be taken
**Vomiting**: hydrocortisone must be given **parenterally**
Carry a **steroid card**, wear an engraved **bracelet**, and keep a **hydrocortisone emergency pack**, trained to self-inject 100 mg IM; take it when travelling

blocks.title: Withdrawing long-term glucocorticoids
items: Crisis on withdrawal is likely after **> 3 weeks** oral/systemic therapy, repeated courses in the past year, or **> 7.5 mg prednisolone/day**
Withdraw **slowly**, at a rate set by the treatment duration; give a steroid card
Morning dosing helps the axis recover; giving ACTH is of no value because the pituitary stays suppressed
Near the end of a taper, check 0900 cortisol, then an ACTH stimulation test before stopping completely

blocks.text: **Secondary** adrenal insufficiency needs **glucocorticoid only**: aldosterone is preserved, so fludrocortisone is unnecessary.
In **panhypopituitarism**, start **hydrocortisone before thyroxine**. Treat tuberculosis if it is present or suspected.

Dose ranges differ between books. Hydrocortisone is **15–20 mg/day** in Davidson but 15–25 mg in K&C (Kumar Box 21.19: 20–30 mg). Fludrocortisone is **0.05–0.15 mg** in Davidson but 50–300 µg in K&C. For crisis follow-on, K&C Essentials gives 100 mg IM 6-hourly and Pocket Medicine 50 mg IV 6-hourly. Quote Davidson.
Older patients on replacement have a **higher crisis risk** because of poor adherence and more intercurrent illness. Repeated education of the patient and carers is crucial.

cards.back: Inadequate secretion of **cortisol and/or aldosterone**. Suspect it in unexplained fatigue, hyponatraemia or hypotension.

cards.front: Plasma ACTH in primary vs secondary vs tertiary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.back: Primary (Addison’s): **high**. Secondary (pituitary) and tertiary (hypothalamic CRH lack, usually from exogenous steroids): **low**.

cards.front: Why is there no hyperkalaemia in ACTH-deficient adrenal insufficiency?
cards.back: Aldosterone is driven by **renin–angiotensin**, not ACTH, so mineralocorticoid secretion is preserved.

cards.front: Mechanism of pigmentation in Addison’s disease?
cards.back: Loss of cortisol feedback raises **ACTH and other POMC peptides**, which carry **MSH-like sequences** that stimulate melanocytes.

cards.front: Commonest cause of Addison’s disease in the UK, and worldwide?

cards.back: Adrenal **haemorrhage** during **meningococcal sepsis**, causing primary adrenal failure.

cards.front: APS type 1: gene, inheritance and key features?
cards.back: **AIRE** mutation, **autosomal recessive**. Addison’s, **hypoparathyroidism**, **chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis**, nail dystrophy, dental enamel hypoplasia.

cards.front: Sites to check for Addisonian pigmentation?
cards.back: Sun-exposed areas, pressure areas (elbows, knees), **palmar creases**, knuckles, **buccal/mucous membranes**, conjunctivae, **recent scars**.
Shock with severe hypotension, **hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia**, ± hypoglycaemia and hypercalcaemia; vomiting, cramps, abdominal pain, fever. Triggered by illness, infection or surgery.

cards.front: Short Synacthen test: dose, sampling, normal result (Davidson)?
cards.back: **250 μg ACTH1–24 IM**; cortisol at **0 and 30 min**; normal = cortisol **> 500 nmol/L** at either time. The increment is not a criterion.

cards.front: Random cortisol level that effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency?
cards.back: **> 500 nmol/L (> 18 μg/dL)**. Lower values may be “normal” yet inappropriately low for a sick patient.
Supine **high plasma renin** with **low or low-normal aldosterone**.
IV hydrocortisone **100 mg stat**, then **100 mg four times daily** for 12–24 h, then 50–100 mg IM four times daily until oral therapy is reliable; plus IV saline.
Hydrocortisone **15–20 mg/day** divided (10 mg on waking + 5 mg ~15:00) plus fludrocortisone **0.05–0.15 mg/day**.

cards.front: Sick-day rule for a febrile illness on hydrocortisone replacement?
cards.back: **Double** the hydrocortisone dose. If vomiting, give it **parenterally** (e.g. 100 mg IM from the emergency pack).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis took prednisolone 15 mg daily for 8 months. She stopped it abruptly 2 weeks ago when her supply ran out. She now has fatigue, nausea and light-headedness on standing. BP is 98/60 mmHg with a postural drop. Na 130 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L. There is no skin pigmentation.
questions.leadIn: At which level has her cortisol axis most likely failed?
questions.explanation: Long-term oral steroid at more than 7.5 mg prednisolone/day for more than 3 weeks suppresses CRH and ACTH. **Abrupt withdrawal** then leaves the atrophic adrenals unable to make cortisol. ACTH is low, so there is **no pigmentation**. Aldosterone is renin-driven and preserved, so potassium is normal. Davidson classes this as secondary (low-ACTH) failure; Zero to Finals calls it tertiary.
whyNot: Primary failure would give high ACTH, pigmentation and often hyperkalaemia.
There is a clear history of steroid withdrawal, not a pituitary tumour.
Isolated aldosterone loss would not follow steroid withdrawal and would cause hyperkalaemia.
The medulla makes catecholamines, not cortisol.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to define Addison’s disease precisely on a ward round.
questions.leadIn: Which statement is the best definition?
options: Primary adrenocortical failure with raised plasma ACTH
Adrenal insufficiency caused by ACTH deficiency
Isolated aldosterone deficiency with normal cortisol
Cortisol deficiency caused by lack of hypothalamic CRH
The commonest cause of adrenal insufficiency overall
questions.explanation: Addison’s disease is **primary** failure of the adrenal cortex, so ACTH is **high**. Glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid loss may come first, but eventually both fail.
whyNot: ACTH deficiency is secondary adrenal insufficiency.
In Addison’s both cortisol and aldosterone eventually fail.
CRH lack is tertiary (hypothalamic) failure.
The commonest cause overall is ACTH deficiency from steroid withdrawal; Addison’s is rare.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with newly diagnosed primary adrenal insufficiency has Na 126 mmol/L, K 6.1 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.75 mmol/L and a postural BP drop.
questions.leadIn: Which of these abnormalities would NOT be expected if his cortisol deficiency were due to pituitary ACTH deficiency?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalaemia reflects **aldosterone deficiency**. Aldosterone is controlled by renin–angiotensin, not ACTH, so it is **preserved in ACTH deficiency**. The other features can all result from **cortisol** lack alone (Davidson Box 18.42).
whyNot: Cortisol deficiency causes a dilutional hyponatraemia, so it occurs in secondary disease too.
Cortisol is gluconeogenic; hypoglycaemia occurs with any cortisol lack.
Hypercalcaemia is listed under glucocorticoid insufficiency.
Postural hypotension is also a feature of glucocorticoid insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison’s disease has dark palmar creases, darkened knuckles and brown patches on her buccal mucosa.
questions.leadIn: What is the mechanism of this pigmentation?
options: Excess ACTH and related POMC peptides with MSH-like sequences
questions.explanation: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so the pituitary makes more **POMC**. ACTH and related peptides carry **MSH-like sequences** that stimulate melanocytes. This is why pigmentation occurs only in primary disease.
whyNot: Melanocyte destruction causes **vitiligo** (depigmentation), not pigmentation.
Haemochromatosis is a rare cause of Addison’s, but Addisonian pigmentation is driven by ACTH, not iron.
Androgen loss reduces body hair and libido; it does not darken skin.
Renin rises with aldosterone deficiency but does not act on melanocytes.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who previously lived in a region with high TB and HIV rates presents with weight loss, pigmentation and postural hypotension. Short Synacthen test is flat, ACTH is high, and adrenal autoantibodies are negative. CT shows bilateral adrenal calcification.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: **Adrenal calcification** is the classic imaging clue to **tuberculous** Addison’s disease. TB is a growing cause where HIV/AIDS is common.
whyNot: Autoimmune glands are small and non-calcified, and antibodies are usually positive.
Metastases enlarge the glands; calcification is not the typical finding.
Deposition disease enlarges the glands rather than calcifying them.
Haemorrhage presents acutely (e.g. meningococcal sepsis) with enlarged glands, not a chronic calcified picture.

questions.stem: A GP audits every patient in her UK practice with biochemically confirmed adrenal insufficiency.
questions.leadIn: Which cause is she most likely to find most often?
questions.explanation: Across all adrenal insufficiency, the commonest cause is **ACTH deficiency**, usually from **inappropriate withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoids** (or a pituitary tumour). Addison’s disease itself is rare.
whyNot: Autoimmunity is the commonest cause of **Addison’s** in the UK, but Addison’s is rare overall.
TB is a leading cause of Addison’s worldwide, not of UK adrenal insufficiency overall.
CAH is rare in adults; it is the commonest primary cause in children.
Metastases rarely cause insufficiency because ~90% of the glands must be destroyed.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had 6 months of fatigue, anorexia and 7 kg weight loss, and was diagnosed with depression. Na is 129 mmol/L. Her GP now suspects adrenal insufficiency.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding would most strongly suggest a primary (adrenal) rather than pituitary cause?
options: Pigmentation of the buccal mucosa and palmar creases
questions.explanation: Pigmentation requires **high ACTH**, which occurs only in **primary** disease. Weight loss, postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia and reduced body hair can all occur when the cause is ACTH lack.
whyNot: Postural hypotension is also listed under glucocorticoid deficiency, so it occurs in secondary disease.
Adrenal androgen loss occurs in both primary and secondary disease.
Weight loss is a glucocorticoid-deficiency feature found at either level.
Hypoglycaemia reflects cortisol lack, which is common to both.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known Addison’s disease has had gastroenteritis for 2 days and could not keep her tablets down. She is drowsy, with abdominal pain and cramps, and her BP is 75/40 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: Which set of results is most likely?
questions.explanation: Adrenal crisis typically shows **hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia** and often **hypoglycaemia**, from combined aldosterone and cortisol lack. It is precipitated by intercurrent illness or missed doses.
whyNot: High Na and low K are the opposite of aldosterone deficiency.
Low potassium argues against aldosterone deficiency.
Normal Na and K would be unusual in a primary adrenal crisis.
Hypernatraemia is not a feature of adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has fatigue and weight loss. After 250 μg tetracosactide IM, her cortisol is 160 nmol/L at baseline and 290 nmol/L at 30 minutes. 0900 plasma ACTH is markedly raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease
Acute ACTH deficiency from pituitary apoplexy
questions.explanation: Cortisol never exceeds **500 nmol/L**, so the Synacthen test is **failed**. A **high ACTH** places the lesion in the adrenal: primary insufficiency (Addison’s disease).
whyNot: Secondary disease would show a low ACTH.
Normal requires cortisol > 500 nmol/L at baseline or 30 min.
Acute ACTH deficiency gives low ACTH and may give a normal Synacthen response.
Exogenous steroid suppression lowers ACTH.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man had a sudden severe headache with visual loss 3 days ago from pituitary apoplexy. He is now hypotensive and lethargic. A short Synacthen test gives a 30-minute cortisol of 620 nmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation?
options: The test can miss acute ACTH deficiency because the adrenals have not yet atrophied
The result confirms primary adrenal failure
The cortisol increment must be calculated before interpreting
A long Synacthen test is now required
questions.explanation: The Synacthen test depends on **adrenal atrophy after chronic ACTH lack**. Three days after apoplexy the adrenals can still respond to exogenous ACTH, so a normal result does **not** exclude acute ACTH deficiency.
whyNot: A normal response can be falsely reassuring in acute ACTH deficiency.
Primary failure would give a flat response with high ACTH.
Davidson states the increment is not a criterion.
The long test is now largely obsolete and does not address acute ACTH deficiency.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with newly diagnosed autoimmune Addison’s disease has recovered from her initial presentation and is ready for discharge.
questions.leadIn: Which long-term regimen is most appropriate?
options: Hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg mid-afternoon, plus fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily
Hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg mid-afternoon alone
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM four times daily
questions.explanation: Primary insufficiency needs **both** glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone 15–20 mg/day in divided doses) **and** mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone 0.05–0.15 mg/day) replacement.
whyNot: Without fludrocortisone, aldosterone deficiency is not replaced; it is needed in virtually all primary cases.
This is far above physiological replacement and would cause Cushingoid effects.
Cortisol must always be replaced.
This is a crisis/perioperative regimen, not maintenance.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with Addison’s disease on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone develops influenza with a temperature of 38.6 °C. He is eating and drinking normally.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Double the hydrocortisone dose during the febrile illness
Self-inject hydrocortisone 100 mg IM four times daily
questions.explanation: Sick-day rule: in a **febrile illness, double** the hydrocortisone dose to mimic the normal stress rise in cortisol.
whyNot: An unchanged dose risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
Fludrocortisone should not be stopped; it is the glucocorticoid that needs increasing.
Reducing the dose during stress is dangerous.
Parenteral hydrocortisone is for vomiting or inability to take tablets.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student presents with fever, neck stiffness and a spreading non-blanching rash on his legs. Within hours he is in profound shock that responds poorly to fluids. Na 127 mmol/L, K 5.9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: **Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome**: adrenal haemorrhage during meningococcal sepsis destroys both glands, causing acute primary failure (hyperkalaemia shows aldosterone loss).

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman is tired and dizzy 6 months after a delivery complicated by massive haemorrhage requiring transfusion. Na is 130 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, there is no pigmentation, and 0900 ACTH is low.
items.explanation: Two steps: **low ACTH, no pigmentation and normal K** mean secondary failure. Then **postpartum haemorrhage** points to pituitary necrosis, i.e. **Sheehan’s syndrome**.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with known lung cancer has weight loss and postural hypotension. The Synacthen test is flat with a high ACTH, and CT shows both adrenals enlarged.
items.explanation: **Metastatic carcinoma** (lung is a common primary) enlarges the adrenals; around 90% of the glands must be destroyed before insufficiency appears.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man in intensive care stays hypotensive despite fluids after a rapid-sequence intubation. Induction used a single dose of an induction agent known to block cortisol synthesis.
items.explanation: **Etomidate** inhibits corticosteroid synthesis and can cause adrenal insufficiency **even after a single dose**.

questions.theme: Next investigation in suspected adrenal insufficiency
questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.
options: Thyroid function, vitamin B12 and glucose screening
Store a random blood sample, then give hydrocortisone immediately

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has 4 months of tiredness and weight loss, with Na 131 mmol/L. She is well and normotensive. A random cortisol at 15:00 was 290 nmol/L. What is the next step to confirm or exclude adrenal insufficiency?
items.explanation: A random cortisol below 500 nmol/L neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis. In a **stable** patient the **short Synacthen test** is the key test.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man fails a Synacthen test and has a very high 0900 ACTH. Adrenal autoantibodies are negative and he has no history of tuberculosis. What is the next step to find the cause?
items.explanation: Primary failure with **negative antibodies** calls for **adrenal imaging (CT/MRI)** to look for infiltration, haemorrhage, infection or calcification.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with autoimmune Addison’s disease (21-hydroxylase antibodies positive). What further testing is recommended?
items.explanation: Autoimmune adrenal failure should prompt **screening for other organ-specific autoimmunity**: thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and type 1 diabetes.

items.stem: Paramedics bring in a 30-year-old man who is vomiting, confused and pigmented. BP 70/40 mmHg, Na 120 mmol/L, K 6.6 mmol/L. What should be done first?
items.explanation: In suspected **adrenal crisis**, never delay treatment: **store blood** for cortisol (± ACTH) and **give hydrocortisone at once**. Confirm the diagnosis later.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.
options: Acute ACTH deficiency without adrenal atrophy

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman: cortisol 140 nmol/L at baseline and 210 nmol/L 30 minutes after 250 μg Synacthen. 0900 ACTH is high. Supine renin is high with low aldosterone.
items.explanation: Step 1: neither cortisol value exceeds 500 nmol/L, so the test is **failed**. Step 2: **ACTH is high**, so the adrenal is the site. Step 3: **high renin with low aldosterone** confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency, as expected in primary disease. Diagnosis: **Addison’s disease**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man had pituitary radiotherapy 2 years ago. He is tired but not pigmented, and K is 4.1 mmol/L. His 30-minute post-Synacthen cortisol is 260 nmol/L and 0900 ACTH is low.
items.explanation: Step 1: the Synacthen test is **failed**. Step 2: **ACTH is low**, so the fault is pituitary. Step 3: the adrenals fail to respond because **chronic ACTH lack has made them atrophy**. Normal potassium and no pigmentation fit, because aldosterone is renin-driven. Diagnosis: **chronic secondary insufficiency**.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with Addison’s disease takes hydrocortisone 30 mg daily. Over a year she has gained 6 kg. Her BP is normal without a postural drop, and her electrolytes are normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: replacement is titrated **clinically**, not by serum cortisol. Step 2: **excess weight gain** suggests **glucocorticoid over-replacement**, and her dose is above Davidson’s 15–20 mg/day. Step 3: normal BP and electrolytes suggest fludrocortisone is correct. Reduce the hydrocortisone.

questions.theme: Mechanisms behind clinical findings in adrenal insufficiency
questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.
options: Loss of aldosterone-driven renal potassium excretion
MSH-like action of excess ACTH and POMC peptides
Adrenal atrophy after prolonged ACTH lack

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with Addison’s disease notices that a recent appendicectomy scar and her knuckles have darkened.
items.explanation: Raised ACTH and related POMC peptides carry **MSH-like sequences** that stimulate melanocytes. New scars and knuckles are classic sites.

items.stem: The same woman also has symmetrical white patches on the backs of her hands.
items.explanation: This is **vitiligo**, organ-specific autoimmune loss of melanocytes. It occurs in 10–20% of autoimmune Addison’s disease.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with Addison’s disease on adequate hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone reports thinning of axillary and pubic hair and low libido.
items.explanation: Adrenal androgens are the main androgen source in adult women, so their loss reduces **body hair and libido**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with a large pituitary adenoma has a low cortisol, but his potassium is normal and he has no salt craving or pigmentation. Why is his potassium normal?
items.explanation: Two steps: low ACTH means secondary disease. Aldosterone is controlled by **renin–angiotensin, not ACTH**, so mineralocorticoid function, and therefore potassium, is preserved.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.
options: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat with IV 0.9% saline
Double the usual oral hydrocortisone dose
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM with the premedication
Hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily for 24 h, then 50 mg IM four times daily
Self-inject hydrocortisone 100 mg IM from the emergency pack

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with Addison’s disease is listed for a day-case inguinal hernia repair.
items.explanation: For **minor surgery**, Davidson advises hydrocortisone **100 mg IM with the premedication**.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with Addison’s disease is to have an elective bowel resection under general anaesthesia.
items.explanation: For **major surgery**: 100 mg four times daily for 24 h, then **50 mg IM four times daily** until she can take tablets.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with Addison’s disease on a hiking holiday develops repeated vomiting and cannot keep his tablets down. The nearest hospital is hours away.
items.explanation: Vomiting means oral hydrocortisone is unreliable, so it must be given **parenterally**. Patients are trained to **self-inject 100 mg IM** and to carry the emergency pack when travelling.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with well-replaced primary adrenal insufficiency has normal electrolytes and BP but persistent low libido and fatigue. She asks about additional treatment.
items.explanation: **DHEAS 50 mg/day** is occasionally used in women with primary insufficiency and low libido/fatigue, though the evidence is weak and acne or hirsutism may occur.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has taken prednisolone 20 mg daily for 4 months. His underlying condition is now in remission and the steroid is no longer needed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate way to stop it?
options: Taper slowly, checking 0900 cortisol and then an ACTH stimulation test before stopping
Stop abruptly, since the condition is in remission
Give ACTH injections to stimulate adrenal recovery
Switch to evening dosing to help axis recovery
questions.explanation: After more than 3 weeks at more than 7.5 mg/day, the HPA axis is suppressed. Withdraw **slowly**. At a low dose, check a **0900 cortisol** (before the next dose), then confirm recovery with an **ACTH stimulation test** before stopping completely.
whyNot: Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged therapy risks adrenal crisis.
ACTH does not help because the pituitary stays suppressed.
Morning dosing aids recovery by leaving the nocturnal ACTH surge unopposed.
Aldosterone is not affected by exogenous steroid suppression; fludrocortisone does not replace cortisol.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has had transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. She has a low 0900 cortisol, a low free T4 with a low TSH, and normal electrolytes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate order for starting hormone replacement?
options: Give levothyroxine alone and recheck cortisol in 6 weeks
Start hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and levothyroxine together
questions.explanation: In **panhypopituitarism** needing both cortisol and T4, **hydrocortisone must be started before thyroxine**. Secondary adrenal insufficiency needs glucocorticoid only.
whyNot: Thyroxine first risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
Fludrocortisone is not needed in secondary insufficiency because aldosterone is preserved.
Leaving cortisol deficiency untreated while giving T4 is unsafe.
Fludrocortisone is unnecessary in secondary insufficiency, and thyroxine should follow hydrocortisone.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has had recurrent oral and nail candidiasis since early childhood. She had tetany from hypocalcaemia due to hypoparathyroidism, and has dystrophic nails and pitted tooth enamel. She now has pigmentation and postural hypotension.
items.explanation: Addison’s + **hypoparathyroidism** + **chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis** with nail and enamel changes = **APS type 1 (APECED)**, an autosomal recessive **AIRE** mutation.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and insulin for type 1 diabetes. She now has tiredness, pigmented palmar creases, Na 128 mmol/L and K 5.8 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Two or more autoimmune endocrinopathies in a woman aged 20–60 = **APS type 2 (Schmidt’s)**, the most common APS (HLA-DR3, CTLA-4).

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy’s gait and school performance have been deteriorating progressively. He has also become pigmented, and his short Synacthen test is flat with a high ACTH.
items.explanation: Primary adrenal failure plus **degenerative neurological** features in a child should prompt exclusion of **adrenoleukodystrophy**.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with Addison’s disease takes hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg at 15:00, and fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily. She feels dizzy on standing. BP falls from 118/76 to 98/64 mmHg after 2 minutes standing. K is 5.6 mmol/L and plasma renin is markedly raised. Her weight is stable and her pigmentation has not changed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Titrate hydrocortisone using a serum cortisol day curve
questions.explanation: Fludrocortisone adequacy is judged by **BP, electrolytes and renin**. A postural systolic fall over 10 mmHg, hyperkalaemia and high renin show **mineralocorticoid under-replacement**. She is on the lowest dose in Davidson’s range (0.05–0.15 mg), so increase it.
whyNot: Stable weight and unchanged pigmentation do not suggest glucocorticoid under-dosing; the pattern is mineralocorticoid lack.
Stopping fludrocortisone would worsen sodium loss and hyperkalaemia.
DHEAS targets libido/fatigue in women and does not correct mineralocorticoid deficiency.
Serum cortisol is not usually helpful for titration, and the problem is mineralocorticoid.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought in with 2 days of vomiting and abdominal pain. She is confused, BP 70/40 mmHg, and has pigmented gums. Na 121 mmol/L, K 6.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Take blood for cortisol and ACTH, then give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and IV 0.9% saline
Perform a short Synacthen test and await the 30-minute result before treating
Arrange urgent CT of the adrenal glands
Correct sodium to 135 mmol/L within 6 hours with hypertonic saline
questions.explanation: Suspected **adrenal crisis**: store blood, then give **IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat** and **IV 0.9% saline**, and treat hypoglycaemia. Treatment must not wait for results.
whyNot: Waiting for a test in a shocked patient is dangerous; treatment must not be delayed.
Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely; high-dose hydrocortisone supplies mineralocorticoid activity.
Imaging to find the cause comes after resuscitation.
With Na < 125 mmol/L, the rise should be no more than 10 mmol/L per day, because of the risk of pontine demyelination.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in intensive care with sepsis has persistent hypotension. A random serum cortisol is sent.
questions.leadIn: Which random cortisol result effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency?
questions.explanation: Only a random cortisol **above 500 nmol/L (> 18 μg/dL)** effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency. Lower values may fall within the reference range yet be inappropriately low for a seriously ill patient.
whyNot: Below 500 nmol/L does not exclude insufficiency in a stressed patient.
Too low to exclude; may be inappropriately low for the illness.
Suggestive of insufficiency; needs further testing.
Strongly suggests insufficiency rather than excluding it.

ospe.identify: **Pigmented palmar/skin creases** in Addison’s disease, caused by high ACTH levels. It points to a primary (adrenal) cause.
**Vitiligo**: depigmented patches, a sign of organ-specific autoimmune disease such as autoimmune Addison’s.
Addison’s disease signs: pigmentation of **buccal mucosa, palmar creases and new scars**, vitiligo, loss of body hair, weight loss, postural hypotension.
CT: **bilateral adrenal calcification**, which suggests **tuberculous** Addison’s disease.
Short ACTH stimulation test: a **decreased (blunted) cortisol response** = adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease); a healthy subject shows a normal rise.
